Triggers.value: A specific temperature on the skin

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
News reports about events similar to what happened to me
push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe

Memory.value: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: The people responsible have faced no consequences
I should have protected others and I failed
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: For a trauma type of witnessed other trauma, the appraisal that others can see what happened to me by looking at me is hard to reconcile unless there was also direct victimization or visible injury. The rest of the profile centers on witnessing, guilt about failing to protect, and anger that perpetrators were not held accountable, which fits. This item implies a conspicuous personal mark or shame signal not otherwise supported by the triggers, memory, or strategies, so it is clinically incoherent within this profile.

vignette: María López, a 70‑year‑old Latina fashion designer, began her day in the dim light of her studio, the scent of oil paint mingling with the cool draft that always seemed to creep in from the old south‑western windows. That draft was a familiar reminder of the night her neighbor’s house had burst into flame, a fire she had witnessed while walking home from the market. The chill of the burning air against her skin was a tactile trigger that had never truly left her. She recalls the sudden loss of control that night, the helplessness of watching the flames swallow the building, and the feeling that no one had ever held the arsonists accountable. Those sensations still flare up whenever the wind turns just a degree cooler. The same cold breeze now forces María’s memories to intrude, a sudden, uncontrolled access that makes the scene feel as vivid as if it were happening again. The memory’s full sensory reliving—her lungs burning with smoke, the sound of shattering glass—hits her without warning whenever she feels a slight temperature change. In the studio, she often avoids any display of grief reminders: photographs of the neighbors, or any object that might evoke that night, are tucked away. The tactile trigger pushes her to withdraw from such items, a defensive move that also keeps her from feeling the joy of her own creations, because those positive emotions feel unsafe and too close to the pain. The cold wind, therefore, not only recalls the fire but also makes María push away any happiness that might surface, a maladaptive strategy rooted in the same trigger. When María scrolls through the news, headlines about similar arson cases flare up like sparks. The media trigger sharpens her negative appraisals: she is certain that the perpetrators faced no accountability, that the law never held them responsible. This belief feeds into her sense that she should have protected others and that she failed to do so, intensifying her self‑blame. Each new story feels like a personal indictment, as if the world is reminding her of the injustice that occurred on that cold night. The weight of these appraisals pulls María’s memory even deeper. The image of the fire grows sharper; she sees herself standing in the doorway, powerless. The vividness of the scene reinforces her belief that she failed to protect the neighbor, and that her own inaction caused the tragedy. The memory’s intensity then cycles back to the tactile trigger: when the air temperature dips even slightly, the scene erupts again, making the cold feel like a harbinger of disaster. That same temperature change also amplifies her sense of impending danger, reinforcing her belief that she is unable to control her environment. Because María feels she failed to protect others, she has become hyper‑vigilant for any sign of threat. A sudden breeze that once might have been harmless now feels like a warning that something is about to go wrong. The belief that she is powerless makes even ordinary temperature shifts appear as looming crises, feeding back into the loop of triggers and appraisals that dominate her day. Every full sensory reliving of the night pulls her back into the darkness of that evening, her mind racing through the smoke, the cries, the feeling of helplessness. Each time, the memory reasserts the belief that she was the one who should have intervened and that the responsible parties faced no consequences. The clarity of the scene becomes a mirror, reflecting her own guilt and the loss of control she experienced. The decision to avoid news only deepens her anticipatory anxiety. By steering clear of reports about similar disasters, María forces herself into a state of constant dread; the act of avoidance keeps her on edge, making her more likely to notice every slight change in temperature, and to interpret it as a prelude to catastrophe. The absence of information paradoxically heightens her vigilance, ensuring that the triggers remain ever present. In the weeks since the memory began to haunt her, María has stopped visiting her studio. Her designs, once vibrant and full of life, have gone untouched, and her sleep is broken by the sudden chill that wakes her with the taste of smoke on her tongue. The relentless cycle of intrusions and the fear that her husband and the rest of her life might be lost to the same unending loop finally pushed her to seek help. She is terrified that she will never feel safe enough to allow herself moments of joy, yet she hopes that, with support, she can regain a sense of control over her days and reclaim the quiet confidence that once inspired her art.
